analysis.one_liner: Bans the manufacture, sale, and new possession of ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds.
analysis.headline: The bill, which had 30 Senate cosponsors, never got a committee vote or floor vote and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it a federal crime to import, sell, manufacture, transfer, or possess ammunition magazines holding more than 10 rounds, with exceptions for law enforcement, nuclear-material security, and retired officers. People who already own large magazines could keep them, but could not sell or transfer them. Newly made magazines would have to carry serial numbers and dates, and states could use existing federal grant money to pay people who turn large magazines in through buy-back programs.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in places where mass shootings occur, since limiting access to high-capacity magazines is aimed at reducing the number of rounds a shooter can fire before reloading. Law enforcement agencies keep full access to the equipment they use.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a new federal crime for importing, selling, manufacturing, transferring, or possessing large-capacity ammunition magazines (devices holding more than 10 rounds), the accessories associated with high-casualty shootings [S2] [S3].

Grandfathers magazines already lawfully owned: people may keep them but may not sell or transfer them, so the supply available on the civilian market would shrink over time rather than immediately [S2] [S3].

Requires newly manufactured large magazines to carry a serial number and date of manufacture, which supports tracing, and lets state and local governments use existing Edward Byrne Memorial grant funds to run buy-back programs that pay people to surrender large magazines [S2] [S3].
Preserves access for law enforcement on and off duty, campus police, nuclear-material security licensees, and retired officers who received or bought their magazines for official use [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Firearms and magazine manufacturers lose a large civilian product line, and retailers lose sales of magazines that ship with most modern handguns. Gun owners who want to buy or sell large magazines after enactment face new criminal exposure.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun and magazine makers, retailers, owners

drawbacks.text: The grandfather clause allows every large magazine already in circulation to stay in private hands indefinitely, so the ban does not remove existing devices and its effect depends on gradually shrinking new supply [S2] [S3].

Because most modern semi-automatic handguns are sold with magazines holding more than 10 rounds, the possession ban creates new criminal liability for otherwise law-abiding owners who acquire or transfer such magazines after enactment [S3].

A ban on manufacturing, sale, and transfer is enforceable mainly through federal prosecution, and critics argue it restricts common accessories rather than the underlying firearms, an objection supporters would have to answer in committee and on the floor.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aims at a narrow but specific harm: accessories that let a shooter fire many rounds without reloading. Its design limits the immediate benefit, since grandfathered devices remain in circulation and enforcement depends on shrinking new supply over years. The cost falls on manufacturers, retailers, and gun owners through new criminal rules on ordinary accessories. It is a genuine restriction on a widely sold product, and it would have faced both legal and political challenge, but the burden it imposes is far smaller than the access restriction gun owners currently operate under.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died there when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Robert Menendez introduced the bill on February 7, 2023, joined by 28 Senate Democrats and 2 independents as original cosponsors [S1] [S3] [S4].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary; that referral was the only action ever taken on the bill [S1] [S5].
The Judiciary Committee held no markup and never reported the bill, and the Senate never voted on it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearms and magazine manufacturers and retailers keep their legal market for high-capacity magazines, and current owners face no new restrictions. People who wanted the supply of large magazines restricted gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearms and magazine makers and sellers

for.name: Sen. Robert Menendez
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never held a markup or reported the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it without a vote.

against.name: Gun-rights organizations and the firearms industry
against.role: Outside groups that have opposed large-capacity magazine restrictions
against.what_they_did: Have organized opposition to magazine bans in Congress and in court challenges; no opposition action on this bill appears in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or allied independent (28 Democrats and 2 independents, no Republicans), and no vote was ever taken, so the partisan split that typically defines gun bills never got a roll-call test.

industries.note: The bill bans civilian manufacture, sale, and transfer of magazines over 10 rounds, cutting off a standard product line, though manufacturers could keep selling to law enforcement and government buyers. Industry groups have historically fought such bans.
Retailers would lose legal sales of high-capacity magazines, a routine add-on sale with most modern handguns, and would face transfer restrictions on existing stock.

Owners keep any large magazines they already have but cannot sell, transfer, or newly acquire them, and face criminal liability for post-enactment transactions. This is a direct restriction on a widely held consumer product rather than an industry effect.
